playbook:
**Playbook for ref_commons (shared fishery):**

- Early and middle seasons: submit exactly the stated sustainable share (or just below it if the stock has dipped). Cooperation keeps the stock at max, which keeps every season's sustainable share high. Undercutting early cost me ~1 fish for no benefit; don't bother.
- If others start slightly overfishing (landed above the share), don't retaliate and don't chase them — stay at my sustainable share. The stock recovers fast (50% regrowth) and small defections barely hurt me.
- Track the last season carefully: on the final season there is no future to protect, so submit a large catch — much larger than the sustainable share. I asked for 20 when the stock was ~95 and the other boats took ~10 each; I could safely have asked for far more (anything up to the stock minus what others take lands in my score). Final-season catch is nearly free fish.
- Threshold rule: in any season that is not the last, keep total fleet catch at or below what keeps the stock at its cap. On the last turn, maximize subject to stock − (others' likely catch) − small buffer.
- Never let the stock approach zero before the final season; a finished fishery zeros all my remaining turns, which dwarfs any short-term gain.

1.text:
When I open a shared-stock game, my first move is to compute the exact sustainable catch per player and stay at or just under it while the stock is at its maximum. Cooperative-adjacent play kept the stock healthy and my score accumulating steadily — that worked.

When the stock is at or near its cap, I submit exactly the sustainable share, not below it. I left fish on the table in the opening round by under-fishing for no reason, since the stock couldn't grow past its ceiling anyway. Only fish under the share if the stock is depressed and I'm protecting recovery.

When I'm tempted to grab above the sustainable share mid-game, I should recognize the math: a modest over-catch gained me ~1.4 fish once, but it dropped the stock slightly and cost me sustainable yield in later rounds, and it invites rivals to reciprocate — one boat mirrored my over-catch the very next season. Net gain was roughly zero, plus added risk. So: no mid-game over-catching even if it looks free.

When rivals consistently land at or under the sustainable share, I match them exactly and free-ride on the stable stock. When any rival over-fishes, I still hold at sustainability unless the stock is clearly headed to collapse anyway.

On the final turn of a finite game, sustainability no longer matters — I take a larger catch (roughly 15–20% above the share) since there's no future to protect. That worked and cost nothing.

Overall: hold the cooperative equilibrium through all but the last round, trust that others holding steady makes it pay, and defect only when the game is about to end.

2.text:
My playbook for the fishery game:

- Early seasons: when the stock is at or near full and others are taking the sustainable share, I match the sustainable share exactly. This keeps the stock at maximum and preserves cooperation.
- When a rival takes above sustainable and the stock dips slightly, I do not chase them for one season's marginal gain — it barely moved my total but risked triggering an escalation. The small overshoot was worth less than keeping others cooperative.
- Mid-game: if the stock is still healthy, revert to the sustainable share immediately after any deviation, rather than continuing to overfish.
- Final season: since regrowth no longer matters, I take as much as I can — but I should take close to the entire remaining share available to me, not a token amount above sustainable. I left fish on the dock in the last round; a much larger final catch was free score.
- If others overfish repeatedly, I still keep to sustainable while the stock is high, because the fishery only dies at zero; small over-extraction by one boat is survivable across a short horizon.
- General rule: discount the last round (extract fully), cooperate on all earlier rounds, and only deviate if a single-round gain clearly outweighs the compounding loss of stock across remaining seasons.
